answer:
Your body has its own army that fights germs, called the immune system. A vaccine is like a practice drill for that army. It shows your body a germ that has been killed or made weak, or just a small piece of one, so it can't really make you sick [1][2]. Your body looks at it and learns what that germ looks like. Then it makes special fighters called antibodies that know how to grab and stop that exact germ [2].

The best part is that your body remembers. It's a bit like getting a copy of the other team's playbook before the big game, so you already know their moves [2]. If the real germ ever tries to get in, your body spots it right away and fights it off fast, usually before you even feel sick. Some vaccines need a second shot or a "booster" later to help your body remember. And when lots of people get vaccinated, germs have trouble spreading, which helps protect people who can't get the shot, like tiny babies.

sources.title: Using germs against themselves: How vaccines work (Boston Children's Hospital)
